title: Friendly Sharpness-Aware Minimization
main_claims: The batch-specific stochastic gradient noise in SAM's perturbation direction is the key component driving SAM's generalization improvements, not the full gradient component.
Using only the full gradient component as perturbation (SAM-full) degrades generalization below the base optimizer, while using only the noise component (SAM-noise) improves it above vanilla SAM.
F-SAM removes the full gradient component via an EMA approximation and achieves superior generalization with better robustness to perturbation radius than vanilla SAM.
methodology: The minibatch gradient in SAM's perturbation step is decomposed into a full-gradient projection and an orthogonal stochastic noise component. Controlled ablations (SAM-full, SAM-db, SAM-noise) test each component on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-18/VGG16-BN, and on transfer learning tasks with DeiT-S. F-SAM uses an exponentially moving average of historical stochastic gradients to approximate the full gradient and subtracts it before computing the perturbation. Convergence on non-convex objectives is proved theoretically.
key_results: SAM-noise achieves 81.21% test accuracy on ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, compared to 80.88% for SAM and 78.02% for SAM-full.
F-SAM outperforms vanilla SAM across multiple datasets and is more robust to the choice of perturbation radius ρ.
Increasing minibatch size for the perturbation step (which strengthens the full-gradient component) monotonically decreases SAM's accuracy on CIFAR-100.
limitations: Convergence proof assumes SGD as base optimizer; Adam-based variants lack theoretical guarantees.
No OOD corruption benchmarks (e.g. CIFAR-C) are evaluated; OOD analysis is limited to standard in-distribution splits.
EMA approximation introduces an additional hyperparameter (λ) whose sensitivity is not fully explored under distribution shift.
relevance_to_rq: Highly relevant to the RQ's mechanistic sub-question: provides causal-style ablation evidence that SAM's OOD gains are driven by gradient noise rather than sharpness reduction, directly challenging the flatness-centric explanation of SAM.
